feedback: If you predicted −9 for x = −3, check (−3)×(−3) = +9: multiplying two negatives gives a positive, so the point lands at +9, level with x = 3, not below the axis.
If your left branch goes downward below the axis, replot those points at the same heights as their positive partners; folding the paper along the y-axis should make the two halves coincide.
If your points are joined with straight segments into a V or zig-zag, add intermediate x-values such as 0.5, 1.5 and 2.5 — the extra points force the bend and show the join should curve smoothly.
If you predicted a straight line, look at the y-column: it does not go up in equal steps (0,1,4,9…), so the graph cannot be straight.
activities.intendedInsight: Because (−3)² = 9 = 3², (−2)² = 4 = 2², and so on, the negative-x points land at the same heights as their positive partners, so the graph is a smooth U-shaped parabola symmetric about the y-axis with its lowest point at (0, 0) — not a straight line, because the amount y increases grows as x moves away from zero.
learnerActions: Before plotting, predict the height of y = x² at x = −3 and write down both the value AND your reason.
Complete a table of values for y = x² across x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, computing each y yourself.
Plot each point, then join them with a single smooth curve (not straight segments).
Compare the point at x = −3 with the point at x = 3: notice both sit at height 9.
State in your own words why the two sides of the curve mirror each other.
activities.title: Plot y = x² from a table that includes negative x

feedback: If you drew y = x² as a straight line, compare its y-column to the y = x column: for y = x² the step sizes are not constant (from x = 0 upward they are 1, 3, 5, 7…), so its graph cannot be a ruler-straight line.
A correct straight-line equation has no x² (or higher) term; as soon as x² appears, equal x-steps no longer give equal y-steps.

Check that for larger x your parabola climbs increasingly far above the line y = x (the gap is 2 at x = 2 and 6 at x = 3) — that widening gap reflects the rate of change growing as x moves away from zero.
activities.intendedInsight: A graph is straight only when y changes by a constant amount for each equal step in x; the x² term makes those step sizes vary — shrinking near the vertex and growing as x moves away from zero — so a quadratic must curve. 'Straight vs curved' is tied to the presence of the x² term, not merely to 'being an equation'.
learnerActions: Build one table that holds columns for both y = x and y = x² over the same x-values, including negatives.
Plot both on the same axes and describe how the shapes differ.

Look at how each y-column changes step by step: y = x goes up in constant steps, while y = x² changes by amounts that are not constant — they shrink approaching the vertex at x = 0 and grow as x moves away from zero.
Explain, tying it to the equation, why the x² term forces a curve while the linear term gives a straight line.
Try to invent an equation whose graph would be a straight line, and one whose graph would curve — and say what distinguishes them.
activities.title: Line versus curve: contrast y = x with y = x²

feedback: If you classed an x² equation as a straight line, recall that the squared term forces a curve.
If you ordered the heights as a steady increase, remember x = −2 and x = 2 tie at the top (height 4) and x = 0 is lowest — the ordering is symmetric, not monotonic.
An upward parabola fully above the x-axis has no roots; one touching it has a single (repeated) root; one dipping below crosses twice.
activities.intendedInsight: Quickly consolidates recognition that an x² term signals a curve, that a parabola can cross the x-axis twice, once or not at all, and that points equidistant from the axis of symmetry share the same height.
learnerActions: Sort a set of linear and quadratic equations into 'straight line' versus 'curve' based on whether they contain an x² term (with a nonzero coefficient).
For each pictured parabola, answer: how many times does it cross the x-axis — twice, once, or not at all?
Order the points x = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 for y = x² by their height to expose the mirror pairing.
activities.title: Recognition checks: classify, count roots, and order by height
